title: AI Metropolis: Scaling Large Language Model-based Multi-Agent Simulation with Out-of-order Execution
problem: LLM-powered multi-agent simulations use global step-wise synchronization (borrowed from RL frameworks) that creates false dependencies between agents who are spatially distant and have no actual interaction, severely limiting parallelism and LLM inference batch sizes.
method: AI Metropolis introduces out-of-order execution for multi-agent simulation. A spatiotemporal dependency graph tracks real read-after-write dependencies: agent A is blocked by agent B only if their spatial distance is within reach over the step difference (radius_p + |StepA - StepB - 1| * max_vel). Agents that are coupled (within interaction range at same step) form clusters. A controller process uses geo-clustering to form ready clusters and dispatches them to worker processes via a priority queue sorted by step number (earlier steps = higher priority). Workers update the dependency graph in parallel using an in-memory Redis database with transactional updates. The critical path is C++ for low-latency controller logic.

title: APOLLO: SGD-like Memory, AdamW-level Performance
problem: AdamW optimizer for LLM training maintains first and second moments, tripling memory requirements over model weights alone (28 GB optimizer states for LLaMA-7B). This forces smaller batch sizes, more GPUs, or lower-end models.
method: APOLLO identifies that AdamW's element-wise learning rate adaptation can be coarsened to channel-wise or tensor-wise scaling without performance loss. It approximates channel-wise gradient scaling factors using an auxiliary low-rank optimizer state in a random-projected space (not SVD). Algorithm: (1) project full gradient to low-rank space via random Gaussian matrix; (2) apply AdamW on the low-rank gradient to get low-rank moments; (3) extract channel-wise scaling factors from low-rank moments; (4) apply scaling to full gradient for weight update. APOLLO-Mini uses tensor-wise (rank-1) scaling for SGD-level memory. The random projection matrix is resampled every T=200 steps. A Norm-growth Limiter stabilizes training.

title: LeanAttention: Hardware-Aware Scalable Attention Mechanism for the Decode-Phase of Transformers
problem: During LLM decode-phase, attention computation suffers critically low GPU SM occupancy because FlashAttention-2 only parallelizes over batch and heads (Nq=1 for decode), leaving most SMs idle; FlashDecoding's fixed-split partitioning causes imbalanced loads and quantization inefficiencies.
method: LeanAttention applies a Stream-K style decomposition to attention: the context length dimension is linearized into LeanTiles (fixed-size KV blocks optimal per hardware), then total LeanTiles are divided equally among all CTAs regardless of head or batch boundaries. Partial attention outputs from CTAs spanning head boundaries are reduced using the associativity property of the softmax re-scaling operator, enabling exact attention with near-100% SM occupancy for any problem size.

title: MX+: Pushing the Limits of Microscaling Formats for Efficient Large Language Model Serving
problem: The 4-bit Microscaling (MXFP4) format suffers severe accuracy degradation when applied to LLM activation tensors because activation outlier values (Block Max, BM) are encoded with only 1 mantissa bit, causing large quantization errors that also corrupt the entire 32-element block via the shared exponent scale. This makes MXFP4 impractical for production LLM inference despite its potential bandwidth and compute savings.
method: MX+ repurposes the private exponent field of the Block Max (BM) element within each MX block as additional mantissa bits, since the BM's exponent is always set to the representable maximum by definition. For MXFP4+, this converts the BM from E2M1 to an effective E0M3 encoding (3 mantissa bits instead of 1) with no change to block size or other elements. An extra 8-bit index per 32-element block identifies the BM position (5 bits for index, 3 reserved). For software integration on GPUs lacking native MX support, MX+ decomposes BM into high/low halves (BMH, BML), each representable as E2M1, enabling a standard MMA operation plus one additional sparse MMA for BMH. For hardware integration into existing MX-capable Tensor Cores (e.g., NVIDIA Blackwell), a BM Detector, Forward and Swap Units (FSUs), and a BM Compute Unit (BCU) are added outside the dot-product engine pipeline to handle BM-related multiplications in parallel with the DPE, adding 0.020mm2 area at 28nm.

title: A Bring-Your-Own-Model Approach for ML-Driven Storage Placement in Warehouse-Scale Computers
problem: ML-based storage tiering (SSD vs HDD placement) cannot be practically deployed at Google-scale because a monolithic model in the storage layer must be retrained whenever any workload changes, breaks separation of concerns, and becomes a single point of failure across heterogeneous workloads.
method: Bring-Your-Own-Model (BYOM): each workload trains its own lightweight gradient-boosted trees model at the application layer, not in the storage layer. The model predicts an 'importance' ranking category for each shuffle job based on application-level features (execution metadata, allocated resources, historical I/O metrics, timestamps). Importance categories are designed by analyzing oracle placement decisions under varying SSD capacities: category 0 = negative TCO savings, categories 1-N = I/O density quantiles. At the storage layer, an Adaptive Category Selection (ACS) algorithm uses a sliding admission threshold driven by real-time SSD spillover TCIO feedback, dynamically adjusting which importance categories are admitted to SSD without needing to retrain the model.
